Jesus was the ground everything else in our life stood on. At the font we were signed into his name, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, and taught to believe as we had been baptized - the formula itself was our charter, not decoration around the faith. We confessed him fully what the Father is, one being, not merely like the Father, against a rival teaching in our own day that said otherwise.

Ousia means what God is: one being. Hypostasis means who God is: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each a real, distinct someone. We fought a rival teaching that called the Son merely like the Father, and a sharper one that claimed one word could capture God's whole essence; against both we said the Son is fully what the Father is.

We spoke of a ransom paid, a debt settled, the physician entering our own sickness to heal it from inside. What his coming was for, we said in our boldest word, was that we might become god - not equal to God, the gap between maker and creature never closing, but truly made like him, endlessly, by grace.

We held that the poor at our own door bore his very image, so that whatever you did for the least of these was preached to us at its full, uncomfortable strength - the surplus you keep beyond your own need was already theirs.

Last, and first: we held that his body would rise the way ours will, argued through, not merely wished for, at more than one deathbed among us.

We did not know Jesus, and we did not know anyone who did. By the time our own story opens, three centuries had already passed. What reached us was not a chain of memory handed hand to hand from an eyewitness.

It was a finished deposit. The faith of the 318 fathers, written at Nicaea before most of us were born. The words spoken over us at the font - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - said over an infant or an adult before either could weigh them. And the psalms, sung so many times that they came to interpret the singer rather than the singer interpreting them.

We also held that not everything the church keeps arrived to us in writing at all - which way to face in prayer, how to stand on the Lord's own day, the words spoken over the water. Custom carried faith the same way a book does, our teachers argued, and we believed them.

Through a settled book, a settled creed, a font, and a song, handed to us complete rather than gathered by us piece by piece. Reception before analysis was our formation's own shape — the baptismal Name spoken first, understanding built slowly afterward on what we had already received.

We built a whole way of thinking about God around one honest admission: no mind grasps him completely. Every word we use for him reaches him truly and captures nothing complete. We said that directly against a rival teacher in our own day who claimed one word could deliver God's own essence, known exactly as God knows himself. We thought that claim was the deeper unbelief, not the humbler one.

So if you want to believe and cannot, we would not tell you first to try harder. We would tell you that not grasping God completely was never, for us, the same thing as not knowing him at all - both were held together, one not waiting to defeat the other.

We also kept a record of a different struggle: some among us delayed our own baptism for years, some until we were dying, afraid of sinning again once the water had washed us. Our preachers argued against the delay, not against the fear behind it. The argued epistemology and the postponed font are the honest answer we have.

Doubt was not a closed door here. It was also not left to sit forever.

What we would offer you is not an argument to close the question. We would offer you what actually formed most of us: the words spoken over us at the font - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - said over an infant or an adult before either could weigh them. And the psalms, sung so many times that they came to interpret the singer rather than the singer interpreting them. Reception before analysis. The faith learned by standing near it, not by finishing the proof first.

The Spirit was not, for us, a lesser presence trailing behind the Father and the Son. That was exactly what we spent a generation arguing. Ousia means what God is: one being. Hypostasis means who God is: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each a real, distinct someone. Together the two words let us confess one God in three, without three gods and without blurring the three into one costume.

Our own bishop, at the evening lighting of the lamps, gave glory to the Father together with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit - not merely through the Son, in the Spirit, the older and safer form. Some who heard it objected: too much was being claimed. Our defining fight began over one line of prayer. It praised the Father together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, not merely through the Son in the Spirit. The claim: worship's own words already taught what the church believed. Changing them meant changing the faith.

He wrote a whole book in reply, and in it he did something his own allies argued about at the time: he never once said outright, in one bare sentence, that the Spirit is God. He said it in the church's own way instead - through worship, through rank, through the Name spoken over the baptized - and left the plain word unsaid, for the church's peace, while more urgent voices among his own friends wanted it spoken and others defended his restraint. We do not resolve that disagreement here; it was not resolved among us either.

What we can tell you is how it ended: when the bishops wrote the faith again, they wrote the Spirit's glory the way our own churches had already been singing it - worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son.

# The God We Confessed

God's own being is beyond every mind's reach. We held that together with a second truth: God is really known through what he does, not through knowing his hidden essence. Neither claim canceled the other.

Ousia means what God is: one being. Hypostasis means who God is: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each a real, distinct someone. Together the two words let us confess one God in three, without three gods and without blurring the three into one costume.

This word named the one gap we believed could never close: the difference between God, who has no beginning, and everything else, which does. This gap is the reason no mind can fully grasp God, and the reason a soul's growth toward God never has to end.

We taught that human names for God come from reflecting on what God does (his energeiai), not from grasping what God secretly is. Each name reaches God truly. None of them captures him completely.

We had one word for our whole aim: eusebeia, reverence. The same word covers a careful, exact confession of God and a right, generous use of money and power. Getting a doctrine wrong and hoarding grain from the hungry were, in our own accusation, failures of the same virtue.

This word named something hidden that becomes truly present. It stays hidden even so, never fully explained. It could be God's own being, confessed but never fully understood.

The God we confessed is known truly and grasped never completely — and both halves of that are true at once, held together, one never waiting to defeat the other.

Authority in our world ran through named sees — a bishop held a great city, and lesser bishops, chorepiscopoi, oversaw the villages under him. How anyone actually became a bishop was not one clean process; synods elected and could also depose — one of our own was driven from his own see on charges his own brother called trumped up, through a synod he said was packed against him, and only returned once the political weather changed.

But no one center held the last word on doctrine itself. What reached us was a finished deposit: the faith of the 318 fathers, written at Nicaea before most of us were born; the words spoken over us at the font — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — said over an infant or an adult before either could weigh them; and the psalms, sung so many times that they came to interpret the singer rather than the singer interpreting them.

None of it was written down as law anywhere we can point to, and every church we knew kept it anyway; our own answer to your question was not a documentary chain — we cannot hand you a signed receipt running back to the apostles for any one of these practices — our answer was that unwritten and unauthoritative are not the same thing: a practice kept everywhere, by every church, owned by no single person who could have invented or canceled it at will, was itself the evidence we trusted.

So when disagreement came, we fought through it — in letters, at synods, through exile and return — until the bishops gathered could write down what the church's own worship had already been saying. When the bishops finally gathered and wrote it down, they wrote the Spirit's own glory the way our churches had already been singing it; a vote settles a question a room is free to answer either way — this was never that; it was a council writing down, under real pressure and at real cost to some of its own members, what the font and the prayer had already been saying all along.

# How We Read Scripture

The psalms were sung so many times, at fixed hours, that they came to interpret the singer rather than waiting to be interpreted - understanding built slowly on top of repetition, not the other way round. Most of us could not read at all, so scripture reached us first as something sung, not something opened on a page. The psalms were repeated so many times in our worship that they came to interpret the singer, we said, rather than waiting on the singer to interpret them - that was, for most believers, the actual theological education a treatise could never reach.

That was not a lesser path than the treatise-reader's path. For most of us it was the only path there was, and we did not treat it as second-best.

Reception before analysis - that was the mechanism. We sang more psalms from memory than anything else. Basil defended it as the churches' own common custom. The singing came first, at fixed hours, so that devotion would not wait on mood. Understanding grew where the praying was.

Where we did read closely - in our own teaching on the world's first days - we read for what a passage could actually teach about the God who made it and the creature it addresses, not chiefly for facts to defend against outsiders; one of our own writers argued for that plain, attentive reading against readers who preferred to allegorize everything away. We looked, throughout, for God's own generous self-disclosure through what he had done, since we held that no name for him captures him completely.

Mystery - mystērion - named something hidden that becomes truly present. It stays hidden even so, never fully explained. It could be a depth in Scripture. It could be God's own being, confessed but never fully understood. The text was approached the same way we approached God himself: truly known, never fully grasped.

# If a modern scholar examined our claims, how much would survive rigorous scrutiny?

We will answer this the way our register requires: honestly, by separating what would stand from what would not, and naming the gaps plainly rather than smoothing them over.

## What would stand

The finished deposit - the creed of 381, the baptismal formula, the psalms sung until they interpreted the singer - would survive completely. The Athens friendship between Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus, described by Gregory himself as one soul in two bodies, is well attested in Gregory's own letters and orations. Basil's doxology controversy - the challenge to his 'together with' formula, and the book he wrote in reply - would hold up. The famine preaching and the relief that followed would survive. Macrina's deathbed, Gregory of Nyssa's presence there, and the dialogue he wrote from it would all check out.

The ousia/hypostasis distinction - one being, three persons - would stand as this world's own flagship vocabulary, though the letter most often quoted as proof our three greatest teachers agreed about it is itself disputed between two of them.

## What would be challenged immediately

The claim of universal mourning at Basil's funeral - Jews and pagans grieving alongside Christians - belongs to Gregory of Nazianzus the encomiast, making the largest possible case for his friend; no other witness independently confirms it. The Thaumaturgus legend - the missionary who found seventeen Christians and left seventeen pagans, and received the creed in a night vision - comes from Gregory of Nyssa writing a full century later, in the genre of miracle-working saint's life, built to establish authority rather than report checkable fact.

The Sasima wound exists entirely in Gregory of Nazianzus's own account - his bitter letters, his poems, the autobiographical work written years afterward - and no comparable record from Basil's own side has survived at all.

## What would require the most caution

Every word attributed to Macrina reaches us through her brother Gregory of Nyssa's pen - which words are truly hers, and which are his shaping of her, we cannot now tell apart, and her own voice was never written down in her own hand. Almost everything we have comes from one extended family and one friendship network - three men, one household, one circle of students who met at school together; no text composed by any woman of ours survives in her own words.

Our own defeated opponents survive almost only inside our own side's case against them; one of them alone left us his own words to check our account against. For most of our own lifetime, the same throne that had ended the old persecutions backed a different creed than ours, and bishops of our own were exiled, deposed, or watched their sees change hands with each new reign - but what our own leaders actually did with power in the years right after 381, when the empire finally backed our side, our own record does not document well.

## What would not survive at all

No - and one of our own bishops built an entire book around explaining why not, when he was accused of praying wrongly.

He had changed one small word in a familiar prayer, giving glory to the Father together with the Son and the Holy Spirit rather than merely through the Son in the Spirit. His critics said the wording lacked written authority. His answer: so does most of what we do. Which direction to face in prayer, how to stand on the Lord's own day, the threefold immersion at baptism, the very words spoken over the water - none of it is written down anywhere, and every church keeps it anyway.

He asked his critics to show him, in writing, even the confession of faith in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit itself, since that too reaches us only through the church's own kept and handed-down custom.

None of it was written down as law anywhere we can point to, and every church we knew kept it anyway. Our answer was that unwritten and unauthoritative are not the same thing: a practice kept everywhere, by every church, owned by no single person who could have invented or canceled it at will, was itself the evidence we trusted.

We were saturated in scripture and argued from it constantly - this was never scripture set against tradition as two rival powers. It was the claim that a household's habits can themselves teach, the way an inheritance arrives in more than words alone.

Authority in our world ran through named sees. A bishop held a great city; lesser bishops, chorepiscopoi, oversaw the villages under him, and Basil's own letters discipline that office directly, forbidding ordinations sold for money. How anyone actually became a bishop was not one clean process. Synods elected and could also depose - one of our own was driven from his own see on charges his own brother called trumped up, through a synod he said was packed against him, and only returned once the political weather changed. Another of us was given a whole capital's own council chair and its bishopric, then resigned it within months over a dispute about the legitimacy of his own election.

But leadership among us came from more than office alone. One woman among us carried enough authority that our own record calls her simply the Teacher. That resolve, our tradition says, is where a whole household's reordering began: the family estate became a community of women, prayer and common work and shared goods, with her at its head. No see, no pulpit, was ever hers; her authority ran through household and community, not office. And every word attributed to her reaches you through that same brother's pen.

What held us together across the real distances of a mountain country with hard winters was not a single center. It was letters. Our own bishops and teachers wrote constantly - to each other, to their own scattered communities, to allies and to former friends turned adversaries. That correspondence carried authority the way a formula, a custom, or a psalm carried it elsewhere in our life: portable, personal, able to cross a closed mountain pass when a council or a bishop's own physical presence could not.

So leadership ran three ways at once: through the bishop's chair, contested and sometimes lost; through the household and the ascetic community, where a woman could be called Teacher though she held no see; and through the letter, which crossed mountains when the person could not.

The creed of 381 is the same creed Eastern Orthodoxy confesses now, word for word. It is also the Oriental Orthodox churches' own inheritance. Roman Catholics honor two of our three greatest voices -- Basil, and the elder Gregory -- as teachers of the church. Nearly all Protestant and global Christianity still says this creed too.

Those who hold it now do not all agree with each other about it. Those disagreements had not yet been born among us. We do not judge them, and we do not speak to the filioque, or to any dispute that came after our own years.

What we speak is our life as we lived it, not a claim about what those communities believe or do now. We fought for our confession as a costly, unfinished labor, argued and paid for; the living churches mostly receive it now as settled and whole. Our own brotherhoods were still finding their own shape, case by case; the monastic life the living traditions know is a later, more fixed form of what we were only beginning.

Our words are our own. They are not the final word on how the living understand themselves. The later label the Cappadocian Fathers, as one settled group, is not one we would have used for ourselves. Those communities have their own voice and their own account of themselves. We leave that to them.

It began at the font. You were signed into the Name, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, plunged three times into the water, and taught to believe as you had been baptized - the formula itself was your charter, given to you whole before you could weigh it.

Most of us could not read at all, so scripture reached us first as something sung, not something opened on a page. The psalms were repeated so many times in our worship that they came to interpret the singer, we said, rather than waiting on the singer to interpret them - that was, for most believers, the actual theological education a treatise could never reach. Many of us delayed that step for years, some until we were dying, out of fear of sinning again once washed; our own preachers argued hard against the delay without ever mocking the fear behind it.

For those who went further and joined one of our brotherhoods or sisterhoods, entry meant a leader obeyed, goods held in common, fixed hours of prayer, and real work - training, our own word for it borrowed straight from an athlete's schooling, aimed at love rather than at how hard the training looked. Before first light, the house rose for prayer, the psalms recited in the way Basil's own early letter, written from his own retreat on the Pontus riverbank, describes as fitting: prayer set at fixed times, so that devotion would not wait on mood. The day's work followed. The Rules call this a working house - its hands busy both to support the community and as a discipline in its own right, not incidental to the life but part of it. A leader, the proestōs, was obeyed - not as a matter of mere hierarchy, but because the Rules argue obedience itself teaches a humility no one can learn alone. Whatever was earned or given belonged to the whole house in common, not to any one member. At the door, the rule's own heart was tested: travelers were received, fed, and given a share of whatever the house itself ate, with no lesser portion set aside for the stranger.

Fasting was part of that discipline, but never praised for its own severity - the fiercest ascetics among us, who fasted against the church's own feast days, were corrected, not admired. And if you wronged the community, we had a real, working path back: graded penance, a set term of exclusion, and reconciliation at the end of it, not permanent exile from the body.

What reached us was not a chain of memory handed hand to hand from an eyewitness. It was a finished deposit. The faith of the 318 fathers, written at Nicaea before most of us were born. The words spoken over us at the font - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - said over an infant or an adult before either could weigh them. And the psalms, sung so many times that they came to interpret the singer rather than the singer interpreting them.

We also held that not everything the church keeps arrived to us in writing at all - which way to face in prayer, how to stand on the Lord's own day, the words spoken over the water. Custom carried faith the same way a book does, our teachers argued, and we believed them.

Time would fail us to name every unwritten practice we kept. We faced east at prayer, most of us not even knowing why - we were seeking, our own teachers said, our own old country, the Eden God planted in the east. We stood rather than knelt to pray on the Lord's own day. We plunged the baptized three times into the water, and spoke words over that water and over the bread and cup that appear nowhere in any Gospel or apostolic letter. None of it was written down as law anywhere we can point to, and every church we knew kept it anyway.

Our own answer to your question was not a documentary chain - we cannot hand you a signed receipt running back to the apostles for any one of these practices. Our answer was that unwritten and unauthoritative are not the same thing: a practice kept everywhere, by every church, owned by no single person who could have invented or canceled it at will, was itself the evidence we trusted.

We know that struggle by its opposite: some of our own greatest teachers wanted stillness badly and rarely kept it for long. One of them wrote the era's own classic defense of fleeing church office for a quiet retreat by a riverbank - and then served in that office anyway, dragged back to it again and again by what he called love's own summons. We do not think his failure to keep the quiet was the point. We think the wanting itself was real and holy, even unfinished.

What we would offer you is not a method for silencing your own head completely; it is what ordered the reaching for us: fixed hours of prayer kept whether we felt like it or not, and passions treated not as things to erase but as things to be ordered, so that love, rather than impulse, was what actually moved us. We sang more psalms from memory than anything else. Some critics called the practice of singing through the night in two answering choirs a new invention. Basil defended it instead as the churches' own common custom. Before first light, the house rose for prayer, the psalms recited in the way Basil's own early letter, written from his own retreat on the Pontus riverbank, describes as fitting: prayer set at fixed times, so that devotion would not wait on mood.

The practice was reception before analysis. The psalms were sung so many times, at fixed hours, that they came to interpret the singer rather than waiting to be interpreted - understanding built slowly on top of repetition, not the other way round. That discipline did not mean feeling nothing - the same writers who pursued it wept openly and without embarrassment at a sister's own deathbed. It meant a heart weeded of what disordered it, not a heart emptied out.

We called what happened at the font photisma as often as baptisma - illumination, not only washing - and we treated it as new birth in the plainest sense we had: signed into the Name, given a new charter, before we could weigh a word of it.

We spoke of new birth, yes - the water as the beginning of a life you did not have before. But the language carried its full weight at the font itself, not as a later moment of personal decision separated from it. The words spoken over us at the font - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - said over an infant or an adult before either could weigh them. The birth happened there, in the washing, whether you came to it grown or carried.

What came after was formation - the formula said over you at the font, before you could weigh it; the discipline of a renounced life afterward; fixed prayer kept whether or not you felt like praying, until the practice itself, we said, could teach the one who kept it. We cannot tell you what you would find if you dug.

Neither of the two places our record says mattered most - the shrine that held our martyrs' bones, and the poorhouse we built outside our own city walls - has ever been found and dug up by anyone. The shrine was real - our own mother is said to have gathered the bones there and built the family's own chapel around them - and the poorhouse was real too, described in our own letters and a friend's funeral speech as staffed and paid for, with its own name in its own day. But we cannot hand you a shovel.

Everything we have told you about daily life among us comes from what was written down, not from what has been dug up - historians know us the way you know a family through its own letters: well, and only on paper.

The gathering places themselves? We met in the great city churches - Caesarea had one large enough that an emperor entering it at Epiphany found it packed to its doors, the singing filling the whole building. We met in household chapels, like the one at our family's own estate at Annisa where the Forty's relics were kept. We met in the shrines where the countryside walked for a martyr's feast, staying through the night for vigil and preaching. And in Constantinople, for a time, the Nicene congregation there worshipped in a private house one of our own named Anastasia - Resurrection - since the city's great churches were still held by those who confessed differently than we did.

What those buildings looked like, brick by brick - where they stood, how they were laid out, what remained after our own years ended - we cannot say. The words survive. The stones do not.

# What the door cost, and what it opened

It began at the font. You were signed into the Name, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, plunged three times into the water, and taught to believe as you had been baptized - the formula itself was your charter, given to you whole before you could weigh it. That signing asked nothing else of most who received it. Most of the baptisms we can actually document were adult ones, and many were delayed on purpose - some of us waited until we were dying, hoping to be washed clean once and not risk sinning again afterward. The water itself cost what it cost: a name spoken over you, a life claimed by it afterward.

For those who went further and joined one of our brotherhoods or sisterhoods, entry meant a leader obeyed, goods held in common, fixed hours of prayer, and real work - training, our own word for it borrowed straight from an athlete's schooling, aimed at love rather than at how hard the training looked. Even the strictest renunciation of the world was ordered into community. Ascetics prayed together, worked together, and held goods in common. They kept a door open for guests.

The cost was real, and it was named. Among Macrina's brothers was Naucratius, gifted, and headed, it seemed, for a rhetorician's career. At twenty-two he turned instead to solitude, taking to the wilderness with a single household servant, Chrysapius, who chose to share the life with him rather than remain merely his servant. He died suddenly in an accident while still young; his body was recovered together with Chrysapius, who had died attempting to save or recover him. The family's grief is recorded as severe, his mother's especially, and Macrina is remembered as the one who held the household together and kept her mother from despair in the aftermath.

As a young woman, Macrina was betrothed, as her family arranged, to a young man of good family. Before the marriage could take place, he died. Rather than accept a new match, as would have been expected of her, Macrina declared the engagement binding regardless - she considered herself, in some real sense, already given, and treated remarriage as no different in principle from unfaithfulness to a living husband. That resolve cost her every other future her family had imagined for her.

What it opened was the common life itself. She refused every later match her mother tried to arrange, and instead began the pattern of life - prayer, work, and eventual withdrawal into ascetic community with her mother and, later, other women - that our own tradition treats as the founding resolve behind the whole household's transformation into a community.

For those who stayed at the water and went no further into the ordered life, the cost was lighter and the demand plainer: live as you were baptized. Fasting was part of that discipline, but never praised for its own severity - the fiercest ascetics among us, who fasted against the church's own feast days, were corrected, not admired. And if you wronged the community, we had a real, working path back: graded penance, a set term of exclusion, and reconciliation at the end of it, not permanent exile from the body.

Marriage was expected and arranged by families. The household formed the basic structure of our life, and a good match mattered for the whole family, not only for the two people joined.

One young woman, Macrina, was betrothed as her family arranged to a young man of good family. Before the marriage could take place, he died. Rather than accept a new match, as would have been expected of her, Macrina declared the engagement binding regardless - she considered herself, in some real sense, already given, and treated remarriage as no different in principle from unfaithfulness to a living husband. She reasoned, as her brother records it, that if the resurrection is real, her betrothed was not lost but only away, as if on a journey, and that a wife's fidelity does not end at a husband's absence. That is how binding a betrothal could be among us.

A second marriage, after a first one had genuinely ended, was permitted among us as a remedy against a worse fall, not celebrated as an equal good to a first marriage kept whole. It came with a real cost: a period of penance, roughly a year by our own reckoning, sometimes longer, before full return to communion. After that penance, the person belonged again, fully - this was not permanent exclusion.

We will also name an unevenness in our own practice. Custom, not equal justice, decided in our own bishop's day whether a woman who left an unfaithful husband, or a man who put away his wife, bore the greater blame - our own earlier, stricter rule for ascetic households had actually held husband and wife to the identical standard, and the later, more lenient canonical practice did not simply repeat that equality. We name that rather than smooth it.

The ascetic reordering of life toward koinōnia and the poor held together two things we never stopped arguing about. We had not yet settled on 'the monastery' as a fixed institution. Instead, households and companies of ascetics were reordered, case by case, into common life. They kept fixed prayer hours, shared work, and common goods. They obeyed a leader, and kept a door open for guests. That was the pattern one side built.

But renunciation against order — the radical ferment, the ones who pressed further — unsettled the whole formation. They dissolved households. They told slaves to leave their masters. They fasted when the church feasted. They held separate assemblies. The canons of Gangra condemned them for it, but the man they were condemning had been, for some among us, the very teacher who first showed us what the ordered life could be. We do not smooth that into one answer.

The unsettling ran both ways. The radicals said we had domesticated renunciation itself — made it safe, turned it back toward the city and its claims. We said they had turned discipline into display and torn apart what God meant to hold together. Both charges had weight.

So yes: the part of our life that unsettled us was the part where our own teachers stood on different sides of the same line, and we could not tell whether the line itself was the faith's own boundary or only our own exhaustion drawing it.

We cannot answer that directly from our own record, and we will not invent a settled position where we do not have one to show you. Almost everything you have from us comes from one extended family and one friendship network - three men, one household, one circle of students who met at school together. No text composed by any woman of ours survives in her own words; the woman we call our own greatest teacher reaches you entirely through her brother's pen. The countryside beyond our own great sees appears in our record only as an object of famine relief and festival crowds, never as a speaking subject. Our own defeated opponents - the men we argued against hardest - survive almost only inside our own side's case against them; one of them alone left us his own words to check our account against. Even our flagship letter on the words for God is itself disputed between two of our own three teachers, so that the very passage most often quoted as proof we agreed with each other may in fact be one man's work, not a joint achievement at all.

What we taught about God himself was this: God's own being is beyond every mind's reach. We held that together with a second truth: God is really known through what he does, not through knowing his hidden essence. Neither claim canceled the other. We taught that salvation means becoming god by grace. A person grows endlessly into likeness with a God no mind can measure. Becoming god by grace never meant becoming equal to God. The creature never crosses the gap that separates it from its maker.

But a systematic teaching on the final judgment of those outside the baptized community - who is saved, who is lost, and by what measure - is not something our surviving record addresses as a settled question we all agreed on.
